The club of Indian listed firms selling over ₹1 lakh crore a year has doubled in five years, from 13 to 26.

HOW TO READ IT
Each card is one listed company whose yearly sales crossed the ₹1 lakh crore mark. Banks, lenders and insurers are not counted. A card shows the company's name and its sales in lakh crore for the year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Reliance tops the list at ₹10.8 lakh crore in sales for the year to March 2026, more than double its ₹4.9 lakh crore five years earlier.
- 12 new names have joined the club since the year to March 2021, while all 13 original members are still on the list.
- The year to March 2026 count is 26, drawn from 4,613 listed companies, against 13 from 3,267 five years earlier.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Sales here are a company's revenue from operations for the year: the money it earned from selling its goods and services, from its own yearly accounts. For a company that owns others, it is the whole group's figure (consolidated), which includes every company it owns more than half of; a company without group accounts is counted on its own. The club is every listed company with sales of ₹1 lakh crore or more in the year to March 2026 (26 companies), and the same for the year to March 2021 (13). Banks, lenders and insurers are left out, because what they earn is interest and insurance money, not sales. In all, 4,613 listed companies (outside banks, lenders and insurers) filed yearly sales for 2026, and 3,267 for 2021. As a check against reading errors, a figure counts only when it agrees with the company's sales the year before (between half and double), its four quarters add up to it within 10%, and it fits the company's size (no more than ten times what it owns). A figure that fails a check still counts when the company states it in its own words in a document we hold for that year (Rajesh Exports and Coal India for 2026; Hindalco for 2021). Rajesh Exports' figure for 2021 could not be confirmed (it fails the checks and we hold no document for that year), so it is not counted for 2021, shown there as "not confirmed", and not marked new. 8 other companies whose 2021 figures in our data show ₹1 lakh crore or more are left out, because those figures fail the checks; each of them reports sales of under ₹10,000 crore for 2026. Vedanta is under the line: its own accounts give ₹78,437 crore for 2026, because they leave out the businesses it plans to split off into separate companies. Tata Motors split in two in 2025: the company that sells cars and Jaguar Land Rover kept the listing (shown for 2026 as Tata Motors (cars)), and its truck business is now listed separately. The members' sales are not added up: some members own others, so a total would count the same sales twice. Sales are not profit, and they grow with prices as well as with the amount sold. This says nothing about whether any company is good, cheap or well run.

October–March is expected to be a strong period as construction and infrastructure activity accelerate after the monsoon.

August price movement:
Rebar: +10% MoM, +12% YoY
HRC: +2% MoM, +19% YoY
Stainless steel: +3% MoM, +17% YoY

The HRC recovery has been supported by tighter domestic supply and improving West Asia demand, while rebar benefited from maintenance shutdowns and inventory tightening.

3. Raw-material picture is mixed
Iron ore: Relatively soft. NMDC reduced prices earlier in response to weaker global iron-ore prices, although it subsequently increased lump-ore prices by ~₹150/tonne in September while leaving fines unchanged.
Coking coal: Prices remain elevated and are a key cost pressure. However, Chinese mine restarts could increase supply and potentially moderate coal prices.
Tata Steel and JSW Steel have an advantage from their relatively lower exposure to externally sourced coking coal.

SAIL has comparatively higher exposure to coke prices, making raw-material costs an important monitorable.

US HRC prices have risen >30% from August levels, indicating strong pricing momentum.

China export HRC prices have remained relatively stable.

European steel prices are expected to improve through Q2/Q3, although European coking-coal costs are also expected to rise.

Global demand is increasingly being influenced by security of supply and potential supply-chain disruptions, rather than simply absolute price levels.

European operations could provide an additional earnings tailwind if European steel prices improve.

Out of every ₹100 that India's 4,481 listed companies earned from their business in the year to March 2026, ₹44 went into new plants and machines and ₹28 was paid out as dividends.

HOW TO READ IT
Each piece is where part of the ₹100 went: the wider, the more. 4,481 companies added together, year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- Reliance alone is 5.7% of all the business cash counted, so the chart leans on the biggest firms.
- 3,061 of the 4,481 companies paid zero dividend, which is why the dividend slice sits below plants.
- 1,701 companies had negative business cash for the year, pulled out of the picture so the shares add to 100.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
Where the cash went, for 4,481 listed companies added together, from each company's own yearly cash flow statement for the year to March 2026: the company alone, not its group (standalone), so a listed company owned by another listed company is not counted twice. The ₹100 is the cash their businesses brought in after paying suppliers, staff and tax (cash from operations), ₹13.92 lakh crore in all. Cash is not profit: profit counts a sale when it is made and a cost when it is owed, cash counts money only when it actually comes in or goes out. New plants and machines is the money paid for land, buildings, plants, machines and equipment, the filing's own line for it (₹6.05 lakh crore); money from selling old assets (₹1.8 of every ₹100) is not taken off it. Spending a company files as other long-lasting assets (rights, licences, software and the like: intangible and other long-term assets) is not in it but in saved or invested, so if anything new plants and machines is understated. Dividends is the dividends paid in the year (₹3.93 lakh crore); a 0 in the filing is read as none paid, which is also how a company that did not fill in the line shows (3,061 companies show 0). Saved or invested is the rest of the investing section plus the cash added in the bank (₹3.36 lakh crore): bank deposits, funds, shares of and loans to other companies, rights and software (₹1.8), less what was sold and less the interest (₹7.3) and dividends (₹7.0) the companies received on what they hold; ₹3 of it is cash added in the bank. A company that pays out the dividends its own subsidiaries pay it (Coal India is one) shows that money coming in here, not in the ₹100. Everything else is the rest of the financing section (₹0.58 lakh crore): interest paid, loans repaid, rent on leases and shares bought back, less new loans taken and new shares sold. It is small because new money nearly matched what was paid out, and it is not steady: without the ten biggest companies it is below zero. The four pieces add to the ₹100 exactly, because cash from the business, from investing and from financing add up to the change in cash. Big companies weigh more: Reliance alone brought in ₹5.7 of every ₹100, the ten biggest ₹38.0. Without Reliance, new plants and machines take ₹43.5 (with it ₹43.5; both print as ₹44 with the same rounding); without the ten biggest, ₹49.4. Cash burners count: 1,701 companies' businesses used more cash than they brought in (₹0.74 lakh crore), and that comes off the ₹100. Counting only the 2,778 whose businesses brought cash in, new plants and machines take ₹38.9 and dividends ₹26.2. Left out: 720 banks, lenders, insurers and other financial companies (for them lending is the business), 30 with a cash flow line missing, 96 that filed plants or dividends with the opposite sign (in the ones we checked the whole investing section was flipped, so their split cannot be trusted; ₹1,635 crore of plants between them), and 4 whose three cash flow totals do not add up to their own change in cash. The pieces are rounded to whole rupees so they add to exactly ₹100 (largest-remainder rounding). This is arithmetic on filed cash flow statements, not a view on any company.

The bigger signal:

CEA estimates India may need 411.4 GWh of storage by FY32, including 236.2 GWh of BESS.

GEC-III’s 50 GWh = 21% of projected FY32 BESS requirement.

This creates a multi-year capex opportunity across:

Transmission equipment → Transformers → Switchgear → Conductors → Cables → EPC → BESS

GE Vernova T&D | Hitachi Energy | CG Power | Siemens Energy | ABB | APAR | Polycab | KEI | Voltamp | KEC | Kalpataru | L&T

⚠️ Important:
₹1.86L cr is NOT ₹1.86L cr of immediate orders.

The earnings transmission mechanism is:

Allocation → Tenders → Orders → Execution → Revenue → EBITDA

For investors, order book conversion, execution, margins and valuations matter more than the headline allocation.
